questions.q: What is a pathogen defined as?
a: A disease-causing organism or microorganism, such as a bacterium, virus, fungus, or protist
A white blood cell that attacks bacteria
A chemical antibody produced by the immune system
An insect vector that transmits malaria

questions.q: How are transmissible diseases spread from one host to another?
a: Through genetic inheritance exclusively
By direct contact (such as touching or sexual contact) or indirect contact (such as via droplets, water, food, or vectors like mosquitoes)
Through vitamin deficiencies
By excessive physical exercise

questions.q: What are the body's primary mechanical and chemical barriers to prevent pathogens from entering?
a: White blood cells and antibodies
Lymph nodes and spleen
Skin (acting as a tough barrier) and stomach acid (hydrochloric acid killing pathogens)
Red blood cells and platelets

questions.q: What role do the ciliated cells and mucus in the respiratory tract play in defending against disease?
a: They produce antibodies against viruses
They digest food particles
They absorb oxygen gas into blood
Mucus traps dust and pathogens, and ciliated cells beat in unison to sweep mucus upward away from the lungs

questions.q: What is active immunity defined as?
a: Defense against a pathogen by antibody production in the body, gained through infection or vaccination
Immunity passed from mother to baby via breast milk
Temporary protection through direct injection of ready-made antibodies
Immunity caused by dietary fiber

questions.q: What is passive immunity?
a: Immunity built over years through personal illness
Short-term defense against a pathogen acquired by receiving antibodies from another individual (e.g., across the placenta or via breast milk) without the immune system producing them
Immunity achieved by taking antibiotics
Protection gained through vaccination with weakened pathogens

questions.q: Why are antibiotics effective against bacterial infections but ineffective against viral infections?
a: Viruses are larger than bacteria
Antibiotics kill human white blood cells instead
Antibiotics target metabolic processes specific to bacteria (such as cell wall synthesis), which viruses do not possess since they reproduce inside host cells
Viruses mutate too quickly to be seen

questions.q: What process describes how white blood cells called lymphocytes produce specific proteins that bind to antigens on pathogens?
a: Phagocytosis
Deamination
Translocation
Antibody production / immune response

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of vaccination?
a: To introduce weakened or dead pathogens (or antigens) to stimulate the immune system to produce antibodies and memory cells without causing the disease
To kill bacteria instantly using chemical poison
To provide immediate temporary relief from muscle cramps
To cure vitamin C deficiency

questions.q: What are memory cells, and what is their role in long-term immunity?
a: Cells in the brain that store memory of facts
Long-lived lymphocytes that remain in the body after an infection or vaccination, enabling a rapid and massive antibody response if the same pathogen invades again
Cells that digest dead red blood cells in the liver
White blood cells that carry oxygen

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a vector-borne infectious disease caused by a protist and transmitted by female *Anopheles* mosquitoes?
a: Cholera
Scurvy
Malaria
HIV / AIDS

questions.q: What is cholera caused by, and how is it typically transmitted?
a: Caused by a virus transmitted through sexual contact
Caused by a fungus spread through airborne spores
Caused by a protist transmitted by mosquitoes
Caused by the bacterium *Vibrio cholerae*, transmitted through contaminated water or food

questions.q: How does the cholera bacterium cause severe watery diarrhea in infected individuals?
a: It produces a toxin that stimulates the cells lining the intestine to secrete chloride ions into the gut lumen, causing water to follow by osmosis
It blocks the absorption of protein in the stomach
It destroys red blood cells completely
It stops peristalsis in the colon

questions.q: What is herd immunity?
a: Immunity inherited from animal livestock

A form of indirect protection from an infectious disease that occurs when a large percentage of a population has become immune (e.g., through vaccination), making the spread of disease from person to person unlikely
Immunity acquired exclusively by eating a balanced diet
Protection against bacterial toxins only

questions.q: Why do some strains of bacteria become resistant to antibiotics (such as MRSA)?
a: Because antibiotics turn into food for bacteria
Because patients stop taking vitamins
Because random mutations create resistant bacteria, and misuse or incomplete courses of antibiotics kill non-resistant strains, leaving resistant bacteria to reproduce via natural selection
Because bacteria mutate when exposed to cold water

questions.q: Which of the following diseases is caused by a virus (HIV) that attacks and destroys lymphocytes, weakening the immune system?
a: Cholera
Malaria
Tuberculosis
AIDS (Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome)

questions.q: What is a transmissible disease?
a: A disease in which the pathogen can be passed from one host to another
A genetic disorder passed from parents to children
A deficiency disease caused by poor diet
A disease caused by physical injury or aging

questions.q: Which of the following hygiene practices helps prevent the spread of waterborne diseases like cholera?
a: Drinking untreated river water
Treating sewage properly and ensuring clean, chlorinated drinking water supplies
Avoiding handwashing after using the toilet
Eating raw unwashed shellfish

questions.q: What is the role of phagocytes during an immune response?
a: To produce chemical antibodies
To carry oxygen to infected tissues
To engulf and digest pathogens through phagocytosis
To synthesize antiviral drugs

questions.q: How do antigens help white blood cells identify foreign pathogens?
a: Antigens are digested by stomach acid
Antigens provide energy for bacterial growth
Antigens are physical tails used for swimming
Antigens are unique protein molecules on the surface of pathogens that trigger an immune response and antibody binding

questions.q: Which of the following represents an example of a physical barrier against infection?
a: Skin
White blood cells
Antibodies
Lymph nodes

questions.q: What is the function of hydrochloric acid in the stomach regarding pathogen defense?
a: To digest protein into amino acids
To provide a low pH that denatures enzymes and kills most pathogens ingested in food or water
To absorb water into blood
To activate platelets for clotting

questions.q: Why is passive immunity only temporary?
a: Because antibodies are manufactured by the person's own immune system
Because memory cells live forever
Because the injected or transferred antibodies are eventually broken down by the body and no memory cells are produced to make new ones
Because the pathogen destroys the antibodies

questions.q: Which of the following describes how antibodies help destroy pathogens?
a: By eating the pathogen directly
By turning pathogens into red blood cells
By providing nutritional energy
By binding to antigens, marking them for destruction by phagocytes, neutralizing toxins, or causing pathogens to clump together (agglutination)

questions.q: What is the primary method of controlling the spread of malaria in endemic regions?
a: Controlling mosquito vectors (using insecticide-treated bed nets, clearing stagnant water, and using insecticides) and taking antimalarial drugs
Taking penicillin daily
Drinking boiled milk
Increasing dietary fiber

questions.q: What does a vaccine typically contain?
a: Active, highly virulent live bacteria
A weakened or dead form of the pathogen, or its antigens, which stimulate antibody and memory cell production
Strong synthetic antibiotics
Pure blood plasma

questions.q: What is an infectious disease?
a: A disease caused strictly by genetic mutations
A non-communicable heart condition
A disease caused by a pathogen that can be transmitted from one individual to another
A nutritional deficiency disorder

questions.q: Which of the following white blood cells is responsible for producing specific antibodies?
a: Phagocytes
Red blood cells
Platelets
Lymphocytes

questions.q: What happens during a secondary immune response when a person is re-infected by a pathogen they have previously encountered?
a: Memory cells recognize the pathogen immediately, triggering a rapid, massive production of antibodies that destroys the pathogen before symptoms develop
The immune system fails to respond
Antibodies take weeks to form
The body relies entirely on antibiotics

questions.q: Which of the following practices contributes to the rise of antibiotic-resistant strains of bacteria?
a: Completing a full prescribed course of antibiotics
Overusing antibiotics for minor viral infections or failing to finish a prescribed course
Washing hands regularly with soap
Drinking clean chlorinated water

questions.q: What is the role of the skin in defense against disease?
a: It secretes digestive enzymes
It absorbs pathogens into the bloodstream
It acts as a tough, waterproof physical barrier covering the body, preventing pathogen entry unless damaged
It produces antibodies against viruses

questions.q: Which type of pathogen is treated using antifungal medications rather than antibiotics?
a: Bacterium (*E. coli*)
Influenza virus
Malaria protist
Athlete's foot fungus (*Tinea*)

questions.q: What is the definition of immunity?
a: The ability of an organism to resist a particular infection or toxin by the action of specific antibodies or sensitized white blood cells
The complete absence of blood vessels
The inability to contract any disease ever
Resistance to physical injuries

questions.q: How does breast milk provide passive immunity to a newborn infant?
a: By providing essential vitamins and minerals
By transferring maternal antibodies directly to the baby's gut, protecting against local infections during early development
By stimulating the baby's bone marrow to make red blood cells
By acting as a chemical antibiotic

questions.q: Which of the following is a symptom of severe cholera infection resulting from fluid loss?
a: High fever and rashes
Swollen joints and bleeding gums
Severe dehydration, low blood pressure, and electrolyte imbalance
Night blindness

questions.q: What is the primary mode of transmission for HIV?
a: Drinking contaminated water
Inhaling airborne droplets from coughing
Mosquito bites
Transfer of infected body fluids (such as semen, vaginal fluids, blood sharing via needles, or across the placenta/breast milk)

questions.q: Why are antigens important in vaccination programs?
a: They stimulate the specific immune response and memory cell formation without causing the actual disease
They kill bacteria directly
They provide instant energy
They act as physical barriers on the skin

questions.q: What is the difference between active and passive immunity regarding duration?
a: Active immunity is short-lived; passive immunity lasts a lifetime
Active immunity typically provides long-lasting (often lifelong) protection due to memory cells, whereas passive immunity is short-term and temporary
Both types of immunity last for exactly one week
Neither type provides any protection

questions.q: Which defense mechanism traps dust and pathogens in the nasal passages and trachea before they reach the lungs?
a: Stomach acid
Saliva enzymes
Mucus secreted by goblet cells
Platelet plugs

questions.q: Why are viruses unaffected by penicillin or other standard bacterial antibiotics?
a: Because viruses have thick cell walls
Because viruses are too large to absorb drugs
Because viruses do not possess cellular structures, cell walls, or independent metabolic pathways for antibiotics to target
Because viruses live inside red blood cells
